claims.claim: Lived-religion research begins with what people do and experience in ordinary settings rather than measuring religiosity only as conformity to official denominational norms.
Everyday religious practice may be embodied, material, emotional, aesthetic and morally evaluative, so interviews about belief alone provide incomplete evidence.
Inconsistency between institutional teaching and household practice is an empirical finding rather than proof that the practice is insincere or analytically irrelevant.
Ammerman’s framework locates lived religion within social contexts and recurrent practices, preventing everyday religion from being reduced to private individual choice.
Hui interviewees’ deference to mosque experts shows that asking ordinary participants for the correct religious answer may reproduce elite authority and hide everyday knowledge.
Ethnographic access to domestic, occupational and digital routines requires privacy safeguards because seemingly mundane details can reveal affiliation, health or family conflict.
Identification operates through internal self-understanding and external categorization at individual, interactional and institutional levels rather than existing as a fixed inner substance.
Belonging is situational and relational: people may attach to family, place or congregation without accepting every official belief or identity label.
Day’s empirical work shows that statements about belief can express kinship, moral relationships and generational belonging rather than only assent to supernatural propositions.
Symbolic boundaries classify similarity and difference, while social boundaries depend on whether those classifications shape access, interaction or unequal resources.
Chong’s second-generation Korean American case documents how ethnic churches can build belonging under racial marginalization without representing every person of that ancestry.
Researchers must separate self-identification, attributed identity, formal membership and observed participation because these measures can diverge within the same person and setting.
Gender and sexuality are produced through embodied practice, institutions, texts and interpretation, and no tradition has one uncontested position that can be inferred from its name.
Mahmood’s mosque-movement ethnography challenges defining agency exclusively as resistance and examines how ethical capacities are cultivated through embodied norms.
Recognizing norm-inhabiting agency does not make unequal consequences immune from criticism; researchers must distinguish participants’ projects from their own normative evaluation.
Moultrie documents Black Christian women negotiating sexual agency through ministries and digital media beyond conventional clerical channels.
Religious authority can be epistemic and relationally activated by lay users, so it should not be mapped only through formal male offices or commands.
Intersectional analysis must examine how gender and sexuality meet race, class, age, disability, migration and clerical status without treating any combination as a uniform identity.
Tweed’s crossing-and-dwelling model treats religion as orienting people in movement and place, avoiding the assumption that mobility and rooted practice are opposites.
Human mobility can transform institutions, gender roles, ritual calendars and authority rather than simply transporting an unchanged religion from origin to destination.
Guest’s Fuzhounese case links religious communities to migrant incorporation, stratified labor, mutual assistance and two-way institutional networks between New York and China.
Transnational ties are sustained through unequal access to money, legal status, media, travel and organizational office and therefore cannot be presumed from ancestry alone.
Diaspora should be reserved for historically and politically meaningful relations of dispersal, memory and collective orientation rather than used as a synonym for all migrants.
Multi-sited comparison must include non-mobile relatives and locally oriented participants so highly connected travelers do not stand in for an entire migrant population.
Religious majority and minority are relational positions shaped by jurisdiction, institutional support and arena, not permanent properties of globally named traditions.
FRA survey findings show that reported anti-Muslim discrimination can overlap religion, ethnic origin, skin colour and immigrant background across work and other daily-life arenas.
Self-reported discrimination measures perceived experience and exposure, while administrative complaints and field experiments measure different parts of unequal treatment.
Cross-national evidence associates minority discrimination with competition against state-supported religion, perceived political threat and weak independent judicial protection.
Intersectionality helps identify combined harms that single-ground categories miss, but fixed intersectional labels can also obscure ambivalence and changing self-understanding.
Internal hierarchy and discrimination within minority communities must be studied without using them to excuse external discrimination or treating leaders as sole representatives.
Rambo models conversion as a multidimensional process involving context, crisis, quest, encounter, interaction, commitment and consequences rather than a universally instantaneous event.
The stages in a conversion model are heuristic and may recur, overlap or be narrated differently after the fact, so they must not be imposed as a compulsory sequence.
Sahoo’s Bhil case shows conversion entangled with gender, care, social mobility, Adivasi politics, missionary activity and anti-Christian violence rather than one isolated motive.
Deconversion may involve disaffiliation, changed belief, altered practice, role exit or continued cultural belonging, which should be measured separately.
Menon’s South Indian cases show that conversion can remain contested after death through funerary wishes, names, kinship claims and state institutions, combining continuity and rupture.
Research on religious exit must protect participants from family, community, employment or legal harm and must not assume that public silence means unchanged affiliation.
